opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest change is going to be in how much we can trust the code we ship.

Right now software engineering runs on a kind of social trust. You write code, you write some tests, someone reviews it, and then you hope. Tests only check the cases you thought of. Code review depends on a tired human at four in the afternoon catching the subtle off-by-one. We've built this enormous civilization-scale infrastructure on processes that are, frankly, statistical.

What changes when you have systems that can reason mathematically, and crucially check that reasoning in something like Lean, is that you can move from "we think this is correct" to "this is provably correct with respect to this specification." That used to be prohibitively expensive. Formal verification has existed for decades. People verified compilers, microkernels, and pieces of cryptographic libraries, but it took PhDs years of effort per project. So it was reserved for aerospace, chips, and a handful of very high-stakes systems.

If AI can do the hard work of producing the proofs, the economics flip. The human's job shifts toward saying precisely what they want, which is the specification, and the machine's job is to produce code plus a certificate that the code meets that spec. You don't have to trust the model, because you're checking the proof with a small, trusted kernel. That's the key point. As AI writes more and more of our code, we can't keep up by reading it all. Verification is how you scale trust to match the scale of generation.

I'd also say it changes what "senior engineer" means. A lot of the craft becomes thinking clearly about properties and invariants. What should always be true about this system? What must never happen? That's a more mathematical way of thinking, and I think more engineers will end up working that way, often without even realizing they're doing formal methods.

Longer term, I think we'll look back on shipping unverified code in critical systems the way we now look at building bridges without calculating loads. It'll seem a bit reckless, once the tools make the alternative cheap.

r001.rationale: The response discusses proving code against a specification and checking proofs with a trusted kernel, but does not state that verification requires understanding the behavioral guarantees of the libraries the code uses.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest shift is that we stop treating correctness as something you approximate with tests and start treating it as something you can actually establish. Right now, the way we build software is fundamentally empirical. You write code, you write some tests, you run them, and if nothing breaks you ship it. But tests only tell you about the inputs you thought to try. They don't tell you the code is right.

When you have a system that can reason mathematically and verify its own reasoning, you can ask a different question. Instead of "does this pass my tests," you ask "does this satisfy the specification for all inputs." That's a qualitatively different guarantee. The interesting part is that for a long time this was possible in principle, through formal verification, but it was so expensive that almost nobody did it outside of things like aerospace or cryptographic libraries. You needed a PhD and months of work to verify a few thousand lines.

What changes with these models is that the cost of producing a proof collapses. The model can write the code, write the specification, and produce a machine-checked proof that the code meets the specification, and a verifier like Lean checks that proof so you're not trusting the model's word for it. That last piece matters a lot. Everyone's worried about hallucination, and rightly so. But if the output is a proof that a kernel checks, the model can be as confused as it wants during the search and it doesn't matter. Either the proof checks or it doesn't.

So in practice I think you see a few things. First, the role of the engineer shifts toward writing specifications and deciding what properties actually matter, which is honestly the hard and interesting part anyway. Second, you start getting verified code in places where it was never economical before, like ordinary backend services, parsers, anything touching untrusted input. And third, you can start to trust autonomous systems that write code, because you have a way to check their work that doesn't depend on a human reading every line.

The analogy I like is compilers. Nobody checks the assembly their compiler emits anymore. We trust it because the toolchain is reliable. I think proof-producing systems get us to the point where you don't check the code either. You check the spec, and the rest is guaranteed.

astra-6.text:
I think they can change what it means to trust software. Today, we write code, review it, and test it on a collection of examples. That gives us confidence, but there’s still a gap between “it passed the tests” and “it does what we intended in every case covered by the specification.” Mathematical reasoning gives us a way to close that gap, and checking the reasoning means we don’t have to simply trust the system that produced it.

You can imagine a workflow where an AI produces both an implementation and a proof that the implementation satisfies a specification. A checker verifies the proof, and if it fails, the system keeps working. Generating the solution can be difficult and expensive, while checking it can be much simpler.

The interesting consequence for engineers is that more of the work shifts toward defining what the software should do. That’s still a hard problem. You can prove that code satisfies a specification and discover that the specification missed something important. But having a precise, checkable connection between intent and implementation could let small teams build much more ambitious systems with much stronger guarantees.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big change is that we can move from asking, “Does this code look right?” to asking, “Can we establish that it satisfies a precise specification?” Today, we get confidence through code review and testing. Those are useful, but tests only cover the cases you thought to test. A proof can give you a much stronger guarantee, provided you’ve stated the property correctly.

The interesting combination is a system that generates code and reasoning, together with a checker that verifies that reasoning. The generator can make mistakes. You don’t have to trust every step it proposes if a separate checker can reject an invalid proof. That gives you a much tighter feedback loop for improving the implementation.

But it doesn’t eliminate the hard part of figuring out what the software should do. You can prove that a program satisfies a specification and still have the wrong specification. So I think some of the engineer’s work shifts toward expressing intent precisely: what must always be true, what failures are acceptable, and what assumptions the system depends on. That could let us build more ambitious software while having stronger reasons to trust it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses proving code against a specification and making assumptions explicit, but does not state that correctness verification requires understanding the behavioral guarantees of the libraries the code uses.
